content: Dental caries is the most common disease worldwide, as reported in studies by Marcenes (2013) and Kassebaum (2015). Despite the availability of cost-effective preventive measures that can be applied by families or community health workers, these interventions remain underutilized, according to Niederman (2015). The impact of untreated dental caries extends beyond oral health, leading to a range of issues such as diminished quality of life, poor academic performance, and other negative outcomes (Farber 2004; Blumenshine 2008; Seirawan 2012; Detty 2014; PR Newswire 2015). Additionally, poor oral health has been linked to impaired growth and development, increased psychosocial vulnerability, reduced well-being, lower self-efficacy, and a diminished sense of control over one’s life (Quiñonez 2001; Finlayson 2007; Mattheus 2010; Adair 2013; CMS 2013). Historically, silver nitrate was identified as an effective antimicrobial agent as early as 1893 by Von Naegeli. This discovery led to its use in preventing ocular and surgical infections, as well as its application in dentistry to treat caries by inducing the formation of sclerotic or calcified dentin (Halstead 1895; Stebbins 1891). The proposed mechanism of action involved a strong germicidal effect and the deposition of silver phosphate salts (Miller 1905; Howe 1917). Percy Howe, who systematically reported on its use for caries prevention, lent his name to the solution, which became known as Howe's solution. Silver diamine fluoride (SDF) has garnered significant interest due to its five key attributes, as described by Thibodeau (1978): (1) its ability to control pain and infection, (2) its ease of application (simply painted onto the tooth), (3) its affordability (costing only pennies per application), (4) its minimal requirement for personnel time and training (taking just one minute annually), and (5) its non-invasive nature. These characteristics have led some researchers to consider SDF a disruptive innovation in caries prevention and management (Christensen 2009). In vitro studies have demonstrated that silver fluoride regimens inhibit the growth of Streptococcus mutans (Thibodeau 1978), penetrate enamel to a depth of 25 microns, and retain two to three times more fluoride compared to sodium fluorophosphate (NaF-PO4), sodium fluoride (NaF), or stannous fluoride (SnF2) (Suzuki 1974). These findings suggest that SDF may have a greater effect than NaF or SnF2. Early in vivo studies on primary teeth indicated that silver fluoride could inhibit the lateral spread of caries (Nishino 1969), while more recent studies on permanent teeth showed that it could arrest the progression of approximal caries (Battelle 1991). These promising results led to the adoption of SDF in countries such as Australia (Gotjamanos 1997), Japan (Yamaga 1969), and Brazil (Almeida 1994). The literature highlights that the most effective, simple, and inexpensive caries-preventive agents are silver nitrate, which kills the bacteria responsible for caries, and fluoride, which makes teeth less susceptible to bacterial acids (Niederman 2015). The combination of these two agents into a single compound, silver diamine fluoride, enhances their preventive effects (Rosenblatt 2009). SDF is believed to work through three primary mechanisms: (1) eradicating the bacteria that cause caries, (2) forming a protective layer of silver phosphate that resists further decay, and (3) converting hydroxyapatite, which is more acid-soluble, into fluorapatite, which is less soluble (Rosenblatt 2009). The mechanisms of action of SDF are multifaceted, involving interactions with various biological organisms (bacteria, protozoa, fungi, and viruses), subcellular targets (cell membranes, organelles, nuclei), and processes (metabolism, replication). Studies have shown that silver interacts with sulfhydryl groups in proteins and DNA, disrupting hydrogen bonding and inhibiting critical cellular functions such as respiration, DNA unwinding, cell-wall synthesis, and cell division. These interactions result in bacterial death and the inhibition of biofilm formation (Wu 2007). The central mechanism underlying these effects is thought to be the interaction of silver with thiol groups (Russell 1994). Countries such as Japan, China, New Zealand, Australia, and several South American nations have been using SDF for decades to arrest caries. SDF is approved for use in many Asian and South American countries (Niederman 2015). In 2014, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved SDF for the treatment of dentinal hypersensitivity in patients aged 21 and older. However, it has also been widely used off-label to treat cavitated lesions, particularly in children. Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that SDF can effectively halt the progression of caries (Rosenblatt 2009; Gao 2016). The growing availability of SDF and the increasing number of publications on the topic—over 100 cited on PubMed—highlight the need for an updated systematic review to evaluate its effectiveness in caries arrest and prevention. A Cochrane Review of randomized controlled trials would provide valuable evidence to guide global decision-making regarding the use of SDF.
